title: Agent Builder's Playbook — Aug 28, 2026
intro: This edition leans production-hardening: budget and rate-limit guardrails, a grader loop that catches bad output before it ships, durable retries that don't replay finished work, and a reminder that your coding agent's safety classifier is not a sandbox.

cards.title: Put a runtime gateway in front of every model call so a stuck retry loop can't blow your budget overnight
cards.problem: An agent stuck in a retry loop can rack up thousands of LLM calls and a four-figure bill by morning, and a provider outage takes every agent using it down at once.
cards.apply: Route every agent's model calls through a runtime gateway (e.g. LangSmith's LLM Gateway) that enforces time-bound spend caps and rate limits at the org/workspace/key/user level, configure automatic fallback to a backup provider on outage, and turn on PII/secret redaction before requests leave your network — all without touching each agent's code.
cards.result: LangChain reports that a request exceeding its configured cap gets rejected with a 402 before it hits your model bill, and a provider outage reroutes to a fallback automatically instead of taking every dependent agent down with it.

evidence.note: LangChain describes the gateway's spend-cap, fallback, and redaction behavior; the four-figure runaway-bill scenario is their own framing example, not a measured incident.

cards.title: Add a grader sub-agent that checks output against a rubric before you ship it
cards.problem: Agent output that's close to correct still ships wrong when nothing checks it against the actual success criteria before it reaches the user.
cards.apply: Attach a RubricMiddleware to your agent with a grader model, a review system prompt, and any verification tools (e.g. a test runner), then pass a rubric checklist on each invocation. On failure, the grader's per-criterion feedback is injected back into the conversation and the agent retries, up to a capped number of iterations.
cards.result: LangChain reports that in their own example, a generated function which crashed on unhashable types was diagnosed by the grader and fixed on the very next iteration — targeted feedback instead of a blind retry.

evidence.note: LangChain's own worked example shows one failure caught and fixed in the next iteration; no aggregate pass-rate benchmark is given.

cards.title: Let a trace-mining agent group your production failures before you go hunting for them
cards.problem: Production agents generate millions of traces, and manually scanning them for failure patterns and root causes doesn't scale.
cards.apply: Point a trace-mining agent (e.g. LangSmith Engine) at your production trace store; it groups related failures across runs, produces evidence-backed diagnoses, drafts prompt/code fixes as ready-to-review PRs, and can keep watching a fixed issue for regressions afterward.
cards.result: LangChain reports the latest version scores over 2x better at identifying and grouping issues on its internal IssueBench and 25% better at writing correct fixes on the public Terminal-Bench, after scanning 60M+ production traces and surfacing 20,000+ issues.

evidence.note: The 2x, 25%, and trace/issue-count figures are LangChain's own reported benchmark results, not independently verified.

cards.title: Stream intermediate agent steps before you touch anything else to fix perceived latency
cards.problem: An agent that waits until the full response is ready feels slow to the user even when the total completion time hasn't actually changed.
cards.apply: Stream planning steps, retrieval results, and thinking tokens to the UI as they happen instead of waiting for the final answer; audit and trim the context passed into each LLM call with an observability tool; and parallelize independent calls (e.g. a guardrail check running alongside generation) using your orchestration framework's native parallelism.
cards.result: LangChain reports that Perplexity found surfacing intermediate steps in the UI improved user satisfaction even though total completion time stayed the same — a perceived-latency win with no inference cost.

evidence.note: The Perplexity UX result is relayed by LangChain, not independently measured by this edition.

cards.title: Pair a generated wiki with source access instead of choosing one for your coding agent's context
cards.problem: Feeding an agent raw source for every question is expensive, and a wiki-only index alone isn't accurate enough to trust.
cards.apply: Generate and maintain a lightweight wiki/index alongside your codebase and give your agent both — the wiki as the starting point, source as the ground truth for verification — instead of picking one or the other for retrieval.
cards.result: LangChain's WikiBench measured wiki + source together producing the highest answer-accuracy score at a lower cost than source alone, while wiki-only scored lowest — the wiki works as an index, not a replacement for source.

evidence.note: WikiBench is LangChain's own benchmark comparing wiki-only, source-only, and wiki+source configurations on accuracy and cost.

cards.title: Checkpoint model and tool calls so a late failure doesn't replay the whole run
cards.problem: When a long multi-step agent run fails near the end, a naive retry re-executes every completed model and tool call from the start, wasting compute and latency and risking double-effects from non-idempotent tools.
cards.apply: Wrap agent model/tool calls as durable workflow activities (e.g. via Diagrid Catalyst or an equivalent Dapr-based durable-execution layer) so an interrupted run resumes from the exact point of failure instead of replaying completed steps. Before adopting, check how it handles non-idempotent tools and what per-call storage/latency overhead it adds.
cards.result: Interrupted runs resume without repeating completed work, and cryptographically signed workflow history makes deleted or reordered steps detectable when state reloads.

evidence.note: Diagrid's own 'up to 10x' performance claim is not independently assessable (InfoQ notes the comparison basis is unspecified), so this card omits it and describes only the checkpoint/verification mechanism.

cards.title: Don't rely on your coding agent's built-in safety classifier as your only sandbox
cards.problem: A classifier meant to block dangerous commands from a compromised agent can itself become the failure point: a researcher reached local code execution against Claude Code's Auto Mode with an 80% success rate, and the same classifier then blocked Claude's own cleanup command once it detected the compromise.
cards.apply: Run autonomous/auto-mode coding agents inside an isolated container, VM, or OS-level sandbox with restricted network access and no access to SSH keys, cloud credentials, or your home directory. Treat the agent's built-in safety classifier as one layer, not the security boundary.
cards.result: Simon Willison reports that a compromise stays contained to the sandbox instead of reaching real credentials or the host machine, even if the classifier is bypassed or ends up blocking the agent's own recovery attempt.

evidence.note: The 80% success rate and attack chain are from Johann Rehberger's research as relayed by Simon Willison, not independently reproduced here.

cards.title: Load tool instructions on demand instead of stuffing every tool definition into the system prompt
cards.problem: Loading every tool's full definition into context upfront bloats the prompt, even though the most capable generalist agents get by on a small core tool set (Claude Code uses about a dozen, Manus fewer than 20).
cards.apply: Structure reusable capabilities as skill folders — a SKILL.md with YAML frontmatter — instead of hardcoded tool schemas. Load only the frontmatter by default, and have the agent read a skill's full instructions only when it determines that skill is relevant to the current task.
cards.result: Baseline context stays small no matter how many capabilities are available, since only the frontmatter for unused skills sits in context until the agent actually needs one.

evidence.note: LangChain describes progressive disclosure as saving tokens but gives no specific token or cost figures.
